name: Mariner 6
payload: Mars flyby spacecraft, two TV cameras and spectrometers (381 kg)
significance: Mariner 6 and its twin Mariner 7 were NASA's second look at Mars, four years after Mariner 4's first close-up pictures. Flying past at 3,429 km on 31 July 1969, eleven days after the Apollo 11 Moon landing, Mariner 6 sent back 24 close-up and 50 approach images showing heavily cratered and jumbled terrain much like the Moon, and the irregular edge of the south polar cap. Its instruments found the cap's infrared glow consistent with frozen carbon dioxide and an atmosphere about 98% carbon dioxide with a very low surface pressure. The picture of Mars as a cold, cratered, nearly airless world, with no sign of the canals or vegetation once imagined, set expectations until Mariner 9.
statusNote: Launched 1969-02-25 01:29:02 UT on an Atlas-Centaur from Cape Kennedy (Siddiqi; NSSDCA). Mid-course correction 1969-02-28. Closest approach 05:19:07 UT on 1969-07-31 at 3,429 km. It then continued in solar orbit (1.14 x 1.75 AU), returning data until mid-1971; that coast isn't drawn. TRAJECTORY (calculated, drawn dashed): no measured trajectory for this spacecraft is publicly archived (JPL Horizons has no ephemeris for it), so the path is a two-body transfer orbit calculated between Earth at the published launch time and Mars at the published arrival time. For modern direct flights checked against Horizons, arcs calculated this way fall within about 0.002 AU (300,000 km) of the real trajectory, but this one can't be checked against data, so it's drawn dashed.
